title: I think AI will allow people to make more than games. I think we'll be able to build entire worlds. Imagine a game where you can walk around your city, every building can be entered, every NPC can act like a real person, every item has unique uses. Imagine having 1000 activities you can do.
author: Present-Chocolate-24
selftext:
I think it'd be incredible to have a lot of depth and a lot of things to do in ONE game. Imagine a much more deep GTA + Minecraft + Pokemon + Sims + whatever else you want, all in one game.

And imagine being able to always add to the game. You're driving around and you realize "oh, I wish I could use a pogo stick right now, or even swing around like Spiderman". And boom, you add it to the game.

You could make everything connected, imagine locking everything behind money. Want to be spiderman for a while? Pay a few thousand dollars. How do you make money? Engage with all the other systems in the game. It gives everything meaning.

**This entire premise relies of course on AI being so good that even a person who can't program can tell the AI what to do and it just does it and fixes its own bugs. The technology isn't there yet. Maybe it will never be? But if it gets there, the things we'll see will be amazing.  Let's hope it does.**

replies.author: cxfoulke
replies.body:
We have to this to a lesser degree with the massive sim player driven games. Like eve, Albion, star wars galaxy was. 

These massive games with some incredible emergent moments. The issue is it's 5 hours of randomly interacting with people and systems till something happens. Sometimes hundreds of hours for the really cool things. 

Most people want to start playing and instantly get into the best bit of a game. Which only really happens in a heavily curated game. 

Personally I don't mind creating the narrative in my mind while playing a crusader kings or dwarf fortress but it's niche. 

Massive doesn't really carry any value. Heck better to just give the illusion of a massive world/narrative for most gamers.

comments.author: YouHave24Hours
comments.body: This is my personal take, but I remember this from a pretty good SciFi book (don't recall the title), it was something along the lines of "The moment you become god, you're damned to be bored and alone for eternity." Imagine everyone at some point has this abilty for "the matrix and world i can be and do everything, i am god", so no more challenges, no more struggles, no more real obstacles... the first "amazing and fun" very quickly will wear off and you'll feel empty and nothing will excite you. Do you prefer video games that have challenges and provide you with a great feeling of achievement and satisfaction, once you overcome obstacles, finally kill that boss, finally gained that abilty, finally solved that puzzle... or.. do you want just be in god mode with every achievement from the start and autoplay? Human evolution ONLY worked through struggle, finding solutions, tough challenges and overcoming obstacles, without this, your brain literally dies very fast (that's proven science). Remember "the matrix"? The architect gave people a perfect painless and struggle-less world at first... it failed miserably. So yeah, that is why i am a lot (not fully) anti-AI: zero effort and "comfort" in everything is void of value and meaning.

replies.author: Riolutail
replies.body: Agreed, you need a balance of both novelty and utility, otherwise there is nothing to chase after the novelty wears off. Players should feel rewarded for going the extra mile to discover something new/better vs just sticking with what they got since the beginning. That feeling has been an utmost priority for me when designing my skill fusion/generation algorithm - no two skills are alike, and all redundancies in the system that I catch wind of are fixed/improved immediately.

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body:
Hey so I actually already have an engine and tech that can generate an entire city along with interiors. Including 80 story buildings that are interconnected by aerial walkways, etc. Its low poly, but i have it working

Do you know what I learned? That space is 99.9999999% unused or will never be looked at. Why would any players stop at floor 43 of 80? They won't, and if they do for whatever reason decide floor 43 is the place to be... well it will take them about 15 seconds to get bored of it. Unless the player has a reason to be there it just seems rather pointless. 

It really put things into perspective for me. I have this cool thing, but is it worth the tradeoff? If this is in the game how much will players really interact with it beyond the first hour or so? Once you learn there isnt a reason to go into apartment 45B on Floor 31... well you aren't going to keep exploring other spaces. I could put random stuff like clothing in drawers but same thing. 

Have you guys ever explored every room in Tenpenny tower in fallout 3? How much fun was it to just find the same old clothes in every wardrobe? These spaces 

So i made a pivot and focused on environmental traversal and created this really fun pole vaulting/grapple hook/griding style of movement. The city architecture is so much fun to navigate and despite having full interiors i never go into the buildings. Because there is no fun to be had in small spaces that have no gameplay focus beyond simply existing. 

  
Just because something sounds cool in theory does not make it fun in practice.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
gamedev teacher here.

I hear this idea all the time, and think it's pretty terrible.

Ok, so you can talk to any NPC forever. Is that interesting? If you know their dialogue is generated on the fly... why bother talk to them? The dialogue is infinite. There's no end, no purpose.  
Enter any building, ok. So? You can do that in real life in a way. Walk into any hotel, restaurant, store. Is it interesting?

Also, as I said before gamers are terrible gamedevs. You basically get Fortnite if you let people do whatever. You're just the 100th person to be Spiderman on a pogo stick. You'll see Elon Musk dry humping Trump, Mickey Mouse with a rifle, and anything you can think of. Unfortunately most of those ideas are terrible.

I'm not bashing the AI, that tech is amazing. But most of the users, not so much.

Tech, in general, no matter how advanced, is an enabler, it doesn't automatically create exceptional stories, narratives, arcs, or experiences. All this one-shotting that's being done puts stars in people's eyes and is a giant dopamine hit, but it's not "making a game", not really; especially not the kind you're describing.

I do believe, though, that the tech you're talking about in the hands of a visionary who can execute can and will absolutely do brand new things nobody has done yet that will be a sea change to the art forms and technical practices behind making games.

But tech does not a game make.

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
Also found this making a game where you can make any size highly realistic planet, where you can attempt anything plausible, with advanced NPCs, and a physics/crafting system that takes into account what the molecules each item/tool is made of in a persistent universe the size of the Milky Way. And the game researched and learned the rules oh how things interact as needed.

I built a lot without actually playing it. When I did sit down for the “last step” after months and started trying to refine the gameplay to make it fun I realized while it was a cool technical feat, what is fun is systems in miniature. I asked: What mental skills am i learning playing this game? Why should i care about a planet when it’s a single grain of sand on a beach? When i can do everything why do anything?

And thats when i realized i didn’t know shit about game design and started to hit the books. Yeah, turns out i should have tried out my loop with pen and paper. I should have miniaturized interesting AND fun systems. Starting with one, and then building on top of that.

The game ui was like opening photoshop for the first time, blinded by possibilities. I was reminded of an allegory a girlfriend once told me about boundaries which was something like this:

*There is a white cliff overlooking the ocean with one of the most beautiful views in the world. Visitors would travel for hours to see. They would cautiously approach the edge, peek down, then withdraw from the scary cliff and leave. One day a fence was built to stop people from falling. Now people dance next to the edge.*

AI lets us build cliffs faster, but does not build good fences. And a good fence is more fun than a big cliff. I scaled down my game, pausing on the 700,000 line codebase and making a version that uses about 14% of the original. Now I’m playing it every day, and not using realism as the guide. Infinite latent spaces are everywhere. A game of go has more possible outcomes than atoms in the universe. A Mandelbrot fractal has infinite shapes. 

The hard parts are meaning (story), pruning possibilities (boundaries and mechanics), and designing an experience. Yes, gazing at the stars is a wonderful experience. But i only do it a few times a year when they’re especially spectacular, and, even then when they’re right in front of me by accident.
